units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
I will give you any sum of money you want.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Even you are not rich enough, Sir Robert, to buy back your past. No man is.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I will not do what you ask me. I will not.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: You have to. If you don’t . . .
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Rises from the sofa .
Bewildered and unnerved .
Wait a moment! What did you propose? You said that you would give me back my letter, didn’t you?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes. That is agreed. I will be in the Ladies’ Gallery to-morrow night at half-past eleven. If by that time—and you will have had heaps of opportunity—you have made an announcement to the House in the terms I wish, I shall hand you back your letter with the prettiest thanks, and the best, or at any rate the most suitable, compliment I can think of. I intend to play quite fairly with you. One should always play fairly . . . when one has the winning cards. The Baron taught me that . . . amongst other things.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You must let me have time to consider your proposal.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: No; you must settle now!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Give me a week—three days!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Impossible! I have got to telegraph to Vienna to-night.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: My God! what brought you into my life?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Circumstances.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Moves towards the door .
Don’t go. I consent. The report shall be withdrawn. I will arrange for a question to be put to me on the subject.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Thank you. I knew we should come to an amicable agreement. I understood your nature from the first. I analysed you, though you did not adore me. And now you can get my carriage for me, Sir Robert. I see the people coming up from supper, and Englishmen always get romantic after a meal, and that bores me dreadfully.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Exit SIR ROBERT CHILTERN.
Enter Guests , LADY CHILTERN, LADY MARKBY, LORD CAVERSHAM, LADY BASILDON, MRS. MARCHMONT, VICOMTE DE NANJAC, MR. MONTFORD.
Well, dear Mrs. Cheveley, I hope you have enjoyed yourself. Sir Robert is very entertaining, is he not?
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: Most entertaining! I have enjoyed my talk with him immensely.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: He has had a very interesting and brilliant career. And he has married a most admirable wife. Lady Chiltern is a woman of the very highest principles, I am glad to say. I am a little too old now, myself, to trouble about setting a good example, but I always admire people who do. And Lady Chiltern has a very ennobling effect on life, though her dinner-parties are rather dull sometimes. But one can’t have everything, can one? And now I must go, dear. Shall I call for you to-morrow?
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: Thanks.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: We might drive in the Park at five. Everything looks so fresh in the Park now!
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: Except the people!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Perhaps the people are a little jaded. I have often observed that the Season as it goes on produces a kind of softening of the brain. However, I think anything is better than high intellectual pressure. That is the most unbecoming thing there is. It makes the noses of the young girls so particularly large. And there is nothing so difficult to marry as a large nose; men don’t like them. Good-night, dear!
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: To LADY CHILTERN.
Good-night, Gertrude!
units.name: LADY MARKBY

units.text: Goes out on LORD CAVERSHAM’S arm .
What a charming house you have, Lady Chiltern! I have spent a delightful evening. It has been so interesting getting to know your husband.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Why did you wish to meet my husband, Mrs. Cheveley?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Oh, I will tell you. I wanted to interest him in this Argentine Canal scheme, of which I dare say you have heard. And I found him most susceptible,—susceptible to reason, I mean. A rare thing in a man. I converted him in ten minutes. He is going to make a speech in the House to-morrow night in favour of the idea. We must go to the Ladies’ Gallery and hear him! It will be a great occasion!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: There must be some mistake. That scheme could never have my husband’s support.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Oh, I assure you it’s all settled. I don’t regret my tedious journey from Vienna now. It has been a great success. But, of course, for the next twenty-four hours the whole thing is a dead secret.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Gently .
A secret? Between whom?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: With a flash of amusement in her eyes .
Between your husband and myself.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Entering .
Your carriage is here, Mrs. Cheveley!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Thanks! Good evening, Lady Chiltern! Good-night, Lord Goring! I am at Claridge’s. Don’t you think you might leave a card?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: If you wish it, Mrs. Cheveley!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Oh, don’t be so solemn about it, or I shall be obliged to leave a card on you. In England I suppose that would hardly be considered en règle . Abroad, we are more civilised. Will you see me down, Sir Robert? Now that we have both the same interests at heart we shall be great friends, I hope!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Sails out on SIR ROBERT CHILTERN’S arm .
LADY CHILTERN goes to the top of the staircase and looks down at them as they descend .
Her expression is troubled .
After a little time she is joined by some of the guests , and passes with them into another reception-room .
What a horrid woman!
units.name: MABEL CHILTERN
